analysis.one_liner: Would let the consumer-finance regulator keep complaints about banks and lenders secret.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred the CFPB from publishing consumer complaints about financial companies, never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau from sharing consumer complaints about financial products with the public, and would have made the agency's community-affairs office and consumer-research office optional instead of required. It also struck the language tying complaint data to the agency's supervision, enforcement, and market monitoring. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on July 28, 2017, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, mortgage lenders, debt collectors, and other companies the CFPB polices would benefit if the bill passed. Complaint narratives that are currently published in a searchable public database could no longer be released, so companies with high complaint volumes would face less reputational pressure and fewer public records for journalists, researchers, and regulators to examine. The bill's sponsors would also benefit politically from an industry-friendly record.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a line to the Consumer Financial Protection Act stating that consumer complaint information collected by the CFPB "may not be made publicly available," removing a public reputational check on banks, credit card issuers, lenders, and debt collectors.

Changes the CFPB's community-affairs unit and its consumer research unit from offices the agency "shall" establish to ones it "may" establish, so a hostile administration could shrink or eliminate research and reporting on how financial products affect consumers.
Strikes the purpose clause linking complaint collection to the CFPB's reports, supervision, enforcement, and market monitoring, weakening the case for keeping detailed complaint records at all.

Frames published complaints as potentially unreliable and "frivolous" in its title, echoing industry arguments that complaint narratives are one-sided because companies cannot always get their side published.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would pay if the bill passed. Shoppers comparing banks, credit cards, or loans would lose the ability to read complaint histories before choosing a company; consumers who file complaints would have their experiences hidden from public view; and journalists, researchers, and consumer advocates would lose the raw data they use to document industry misconduct. The public would also lose the guaranteed consumer-research function the bill made optional.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers filing complaints and the public

drawbacks.text: Consumers choosing a bank, credit card, or lender would no longer be able to see other customers' complaint histories, and consumers who file complaints would lose the public record of what happened to them.

Companies with heavy complaint volumes would face less pressure to resolve them, since the bill strikes the link between complaint data and the CFPB's supervision, enforcement, and market monitoring, in addition to barring public release.

The strongest good-faith argument for the bill is privacy and fairness: raw complaints can contain personal information and unverified allegations, and its title argues that some claims are frivolous. But the bill as written bars public release of the information generally, rather than adding narrower safeguards for privacy or company responses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to industry is modest and the cost falls squarely on ordinary consumers: less information when choosing financial products, less public evidence of misconduct, and a weakened agency research function. The privacy rationale in the bill's title addresses a real concern, but the bill's remedy is a blanket ban on public release rather than a narrow privacy fix, so the public loses far more than complainants' privacy is worth.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. David Kustoff (R-TN) introduced the bill on July 28, 2017, with one Republican cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day; that was the last action of any kind.
The committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor, and no vote was ever taken on the bill in either chamber.

The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and all bills not passed expire, so the CFPB's requirement to collect and use complaint data — and the rule changes the bill sought — remained as they were.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers came out ahead: because the bill never became law, the CFPB's public complaint database, its community-affairs and research units, and the use of complaints in supervision and enforcement all stayed in place. The banks, lenders, and debt collectors the bill was written to shield gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, whose complaint records stayed public

for.name: Rep. David Kustoff
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill to bar public release of CFPB consumer complaint data.

for.name: 1 House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat at referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no vote split exists; both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans, and the bill died in a Republican-held committee without any recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer lenders
industries.note: The bill would have kept consumer complaints about them out of the CFPB's public database, reducing reputational pressure to resolve disputes and removing a record consumers use to shop for products. Because the bill died, they gained nothing.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and consumer financial services firms
industries.note: These firms are frequent subjects of CFPB complaints; hiding complaint data would have shielded them from public scrutiny and from complaints being used to flag supervision and enforcement targets. The bill never advanced, so the scrutiny remained.

industries.industry: Consumer research and consumer advocacy organizations
industries.note: The bill would have cut off public complaint data and made the CFPB's consumer research unit optional, starving analysts and advocates of the evidence they use to document industry practices. Because the bill died, access to the data continued.
